title: Which jobs belong in the UK’s next retail payments infrastructure?
summary: A shop and a direct debit originator may need different payment services, yet both need to know whether an instruction has been accepted and how it will settle. The Retail Payments Infrastructure Board’s response to its June consultation uses that distinction to define a prospective common infrastructure for UK retail payments. The Board proposes a system that can serve different products through common access, messaging and settlement coordination. The rules for a particular product and the experience offered to customers could develop separately. The November response records design proposals for further testing and a high-level blueprint due for handover in spring 2027. Day-to-day resilience of the existing infrastructure remains a priority throughout the transition (foreword and §§1, 4–5).

The evidence consists of 121 written responses to 18 questions and eight subquestions, supplemented by meetings and roundtables. Table A records 110 organisational and 11 individual responses. Technology, data, identity and solution providers accounted for 22% of responses, and payments firms, schemes and infrastructure providers for 21%. Banks and building societies supplied 8% and merchants 4%, under the Board’s classification. Bank staff reviewed the submissions, considered their reasoning and reported themes in aggregate. Those shares describe who wrote in. They do not measure support among UK consumers for a particular payment method (§2).

Respondents generally supported a relatively thin common core. Disagreement concerned where shared services such as directories, fraud prevention or identity services should sit, how different forms of money could interoperate and who would provide consumer protections. A common capability can save firms from duplicating work and support consistent performance. Locating too many functions in the centre can reduce room for competing propositions to develop. Respondents also raised adoption, merchant acceptance, commercial viability and the needs of vulnerable users. The infrastructure can enable a product without settling how liability, customer support or access will work in practice (§§3–4).

The Board proposes a modular architecture with secure access options and a common ISO 20022 messaging baseline. A product could extend the baseline where its service needs additional information. An orchestration layer would validate, route and sequence payments, including batches. It could temporarily accommodate legacy Faster Payments and Bacs formats during migration. Decisions about how to preserve Direct Debit mandates and manage parallel running would still be needed. Respondents differed on the use of mandates and deadlines and on the priority of account-to-account payments at the point of sale (§§3–4).

Liquidity illustrates the proposed division of responsibilities. The Board wants participants to be able to use their own liquidity across the arrangements in which they participate. The core would promptly accept or reject a payment and commit to seeking settlement for accepted instructions through the Bank’s RTGS service. The Bank considers prefunded net settlement suitable for most products currently envisaged, while some respondents favoured settlement instruction by instruction or a hybrid. More frequent net cycles could reduce liquidity requirements. A commitment to seek settlement and final settlement in central bank money remain different events (§4).

The Board and Design Authority will work with industry and end-user representatives to refine the blueprint. The industry-led Delivery Company is then expected to take responsibility for detailed design, procurement, build and implementation, with arrangements for continuing assurance. The boundary questions left open in the consultation matter at that handover. A common service needs a named operator and a way to pay for it. A product-specific obligation needs a scheme and participants capable of meeting it (§§4–5).

questions.question: How much liquidity would participants save by sharing it across product arrangements?
questions.detail: Use anonymised, time-stamped settlement obligations and prefunding records from participants that use multiple schemes. Replay the same day’s instructions under separate pools and a shared pool, varying the frequency of net settlement. Compare peak funding needs, payment acceptance and exposure during a delayed cycle, including results for smaller participants with less diverse flows.

questions.question: Which capabilities genuinely need common provision?
questions.detail: Seek the anonymised consultation responses, design authority decision records and costed alternatives for candidate services such as aliases or fraud data. For each, identify which parties must participate for it to work, how users can switch providers and who handles mistakes. Compare the cost of duplicating a capability with the consequences of depending on one operator.

questions.question: Can a migration preserve existing payment authorities and useful consumer protections?
questions.detail: Use representative direct debit mandates, merchant procedures, customer dispute records and monitored pilots to trace recurring payments from enrolment through disputes and refunds. Include vulnerable users and firms with older systems. Measure failed collections, duplicate instructions, time to resolution and the cost of running parallel systems. Feed results into proposed milestones before deciding on a retirement date for a legacy service. Verify that each affected user can obtain a timely correction after migration.
